specPoints.text: understand how the sex of a person is controlled by one pair of chromosomes, XX in a female and XY in a male
describe the determination of the sex of offspring at fertilisation, using a genetic diagram

primer.text: Sex is the one characteristic decided by a whole chromosome pair rather than scattered genes. This note fixes the karyotypes — XX female, XY male — explains why the father's sperm settles the question, and draws the sex Punnett square whose fifty-fifty split keeps the population balanced.

lessons.title: One Pair Decides
lessons.opening: One chromosome pair decides biological sex: females carry two X chromosomes, males carry one X and one Y, and because only a father can donate a Y chromosome, the sperm cell he contributes settles the question.
keyPoints: Sex is determined by one chromosome pair rather than scattered genes.
Females have two X chromosomes; males have an X and a Y.
Only the father can pass on a Y chromosome.
The karyogram pictures the sex chromosomes of each sex.

low.restatement: Two X chromosomes make a female; an X plus a Y makes a male.
low.analogy: One seat is always filled by the mother's X; the second seat is where the father plays his card.
low.examPointer: The father determines sex because he alone donates Y.

medium.restatement: The decisive feature is chromosomal scale: one whole pair, not a gene or two, controls the trait.
medium.analogy: A switch the size of a control panel rather than a single button.
medium.examPointer: Contrast this with other characteristics decided by one or a few genes.

check.stem: Which chromosome combination marks a biological female?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That combination marks a male.
That karyotype is not part of the taught account.
A Y alone never forms a viable combination here.

check.stem: Which parent, father or mother, determines the sex of a child?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
She can only pass on an X chromosome.
Only the father can contribute a Y.
Eggs carry no Y to choose.

check.stem: What can a mother contribute to the sex chromosome pair?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Only the father produces Y-bearing gametes.
The mother has no Y chromosome.
The egg always contributes an X.

check.stem: How does sex determination differ from characteristics controlled by ordinary genes?

options.text: An entire chromosome pair controls it, not one or a few genes
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
That describes ordinary characteristics.
Sex is chromosomal at fertilisation.
The chromosomal scale is the taught contrast.

check.stem: What does the karyogram figure display?

options.text: The sex chromosomes possessed by a biological female and a biological male
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The figure highlights the sex chromosomes.
Pedigrees belong to a different note.

options.text: A Punnett square of eye colour
options.explanation: Eye colour is unrelated here.

check.stem: State the sex chromosome pair for each sex.
check.modelAnswer: Females carry XX and males carry XY.

check.stem: Why is the father said to determine sex?
check.modelAnswer: Only he can pass on a Y chromosome, so his sperm decides whether the child is XX or XY.

check.stem: Explain why the mother cannot determine the sex of her child.
check.modelAnswer: Her eggs carry only X chromosomes, so whichever egg is fertilised, the sex-deciding Y, when present, must come from the father.

check.stem: A son inherits his Y chromosome from one parent only. Name that parent and state the chromosome the other parent contributed.
check.modelAnswer: The Y came from his father, and his mother contributed the X chromosome of the pair.

lessons.title: Drawing the Sex Cross
sourceHeadings: Genetic diagrams showing determination of sex
lessons.opening: Draw the sex cross like any other Punnett square, with X and Y taking the allele seats: the mother's X meets the father's X or Y, the grid splits half XX and half XY, and each pregnancy stands at fifty-fifty.
keyPoints: The mother contributes X to every egg.
The father contributes either X or Y to each sperm.
The square shows XX and XY outcomes in equal numbers.
X from both parents gives a female; Y from the father gives a male.
The X and Y chromosomes replace alleles in the diagram boxes.

low.restatement: Every pregnancy is a fresh coin toss between XX and XY.
low.analogy: A two-door raffle where both doors are equally likely each time.
low.examPointer: Answer fifty percent, or one half, for any single pregnancy.

medium.restatement: Equal X and Y sperm production plus random fertilisation yields the balanced sex ratio across populations.
medium.analogy: Two equal queues at a gate, entered at random, keep the numbers even.
medium.examPointer: Stress that family history does not shift the next pregnancy's odds.

check.stem: What fills the boxes of a sex-determination Punnett square?

options.text: The X and Y chromosomes themselves
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Height genes play no part here.
Blood group belongs to another gene.
The boxes hold chromosomes, standing in for alleles.

check.stem: What ratio of sexes does the XX crossed with XY grid predict?

options.text: One female to one male, so fifty-fifty
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Half the sperm carry Y.
No three-to-one skew exists in this cross.
The four boxes split evenly.

check.stem: Which pairing of chromosomes gives the male outcome?

options.text: X from the mother and Y from the father
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That pairing gives XX, a female.

options.text: Y from the mother and X from the father
options.explanation: The mother never donates Y.
The mother has no Y to give.

check.stem: A couple has four sons already. What does the sex square predict for their next pregnancy?

options.text: Still a fifty percent chance of a girl, since each fertilisation is independent
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Past outcomes do not force the next one.
Independence cuts both ways.

options.text: The chance dropped to a quarter
options.explanation: No cumulative penalty applies.

check.stem: Why is the diagram's outcome called random?

options.text: Which sperm fertilises the egg is a matter of chance
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
No selection occurs.
Parents cannot choose.
The grid only lists equal possibilities.

check.stem: Complete the sex cross: mother XX, father XY. State the offspring outcomes.
check.modelAnswer: Eggs all carry X; sperm carry X or Y; offspring are half XX female and half XY male.

check.stem: State the probability that any one pregnancy yields a male.
check.modelAnswer: The probability is one half, or 50 percent.

check.stem: Explain why the sex ratio stays balanced across whole populations.
check.modelAnswer: Each father produces X and Y sperm in equal numbers and fertilisation is random, so the two outcomes pair off evenly in the long run.

check.stem: A couple with three daughters hopes for a son. Using the taught diagram, state the chance their next child is a boy.
check.modelAnswer: The chance is 50 percent, because every pregnancy draws independently between the father's X-bearing and Y-bearing sperm.

glossary.definition: The chromosome pair, X and Y, that determines biological sex.

The chromosome only males carry, donated solely by the father.
